name: Esan
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 9 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Rolle, Nicholas. 2010. On the syntactic distribution and morphological form of resumptive pronouns in Esan. M.A. forum paper, University of Toronto; Toronto Working Papers in Linguistics, MA Forum Papers (https://twpl.library.utoronto.ca/index.php/twpl/article/view/15175).
catalog_locator: Section 2.4 'Overview of the phonology', p. 26 (heading on p. 25; pp. 25-26)
catalog_quote: Esan has at least two contrastive tones high (H) and low (L). Nouns exhibit inherent tonal specification, though verbs do not. Tone in Esan is not as lexically important as in other West African languages (i.e. Yoruba). Grammatically however, Esan maintains tonal patterns which distinguish declarative from interrogative sentences, affirmative from negative sentences, and past from present (non-past) tenses.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Esan is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with lexical tone on nouns and grammatical tone on the clause; no opened source says anything about word stress or accent, either its position or its absence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only accent-placement statement in the corpus (Thomas 1910 pp. 141-142, penultimate dynamic accent) is about Edo/Bini proper, not Esan.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone on nouns and sentence-level grammatical tone; description based on the Ogwa dialect (Esan West LGA) with other Esan dialects consulted; citation-form vs phrase-level stress not discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Rolle 2010 (the quoted source) describes the Ogwa dialect of Esan (Esan West LGA), with speakers of other Esan dialects consulted; Rolle notes 25-40 dialects. Thomas 1910's Ishan texts are from Irua. Glottolog esan1238 has no separate dialect codes that I could confirm. The only accent-placement statement encountered (Thomas 1910, 'Accent and tone', pp. 141-142: dynamic accent normally penultimate) is for Edo/Bini proper (bini1246) and must not be attributed to Esan.

sources.note: The section 'Accent and tone' (pp. 141-142) belongs to the EDO (Bini) GRAMMAR: 'The dynamic accent falls normally on the penultimate, but in words ending in ia, ie, oa, ua, etc., it usually falls on the antepenultimate' and 'two tones, the high and the low'. Transliteration key defines a stress mark 'Dynamic accent (stress)'.

sources.citation: Yuka, Constantine Lenzdemo & Evarista Ofure Ikoyo-Eweto. 2020. Syllabic and Tonal Patterns of Esan Serial Verb Constructions. Journal of the Linguistic Association of Nigeria (JOLAN) 23(1): 70-86.
sources.quote: Following Ejele (2003) and Ikoyo-Eweto, (2005) Esan features pitch contrasts on lexical items. This occurrence is illustrated in 2. [...] Two level tones, (high, low), and the falling contour tone are identified for Esan at the systematic phonetic level of representation. [...] Following Ikoyo-Eweto (2016), Nouns in Esan are mostly bisyllabic and trisyllabic. Bisyllabic nouns exhibit four tonal combinations: LL, HL, LHL and HHL. [...] Ikoyo-Eweto (2016) draws attention to the grammatical role of tone in Esan and emphasizes the interaction of tone and time relations in the language.
sources.note: States the Esan tone system before analysing SVC tone: a register tone language with two level tones (H, L) plus a falling contour at the systematic-phonetic level, lexical minimal pairs (efE 'rat' HL vs 'edge' LL; Okpa 'one' LH vs 'cock' LL), bisyllabic noun melodies LL/HL/LHL/HHL, all-L citation pattern on verbs/adjunctives/pronouns, and grammatical tone (tone-tense/aspect interaction); then shows underlying L-toned serial verbs surfacing HL/LH/all-H in declaratives, imperatives and the habitual, with H spreading from adjacent tone-bearing units (autosegmental account).
